vignette:
He is a 66-year-old European man who has spent most of his adult life trying to keep himself orderly, capable, and hard to surprise. He comes across as calm and articulate, the kind of software engineer who learned early how to work with systems, fix errors, and keep things running. Over time, it becomes clear that this way of moving through the world has also served another purpose: it helps him stay ahead of feelings that still feel dangerous.

He grows up in a home where his caregiver is unpredictable and frightening. As a child, he learns to read the air in the house the way other children learn to read stories. A slammed cabinet, a heavier set to the footsteps in the hall, the wrong answer to a simple question—these can mean pain. The abuse is physical and humiliating, and it teaches him that his body is not entirely his own. He remembers bracing himself before the blows land, tightening his shoulders, making himself small. He also remembers the odd, unfinished hope that if he is quiet enough, smart enough, or useful enough, maybe the day will pass without incident.

As he gets older, he becomes skilled at anticipation. He notices the tone of a voice before the words matter. He watches hands, exits, facial expressions. In school, he is bright and precise, drawn to computers because they are logical and predictable. Code offers him something his home life never does: if he inputs the right sequence, the machine responds in a way he can understand. He builds a life around competence. He works hard, earns respect, marries, and raises a family. From the outside, he appears steady, even self-contained. Inside, he continues to live with the assumption that danger may arrive without warning.

In adulthood, the memories do not disappear so much as they wait. Certain sensations bring them forward. The sound of a sudden bang in the house, a raised voice from another room, or the feeling of being cornered in a disagreement can cause his chest to tighten and his mind to go blank for a few moments. He says he does not always remember the details first; what comes first is the bodily certainty that something bad is about to happen. When startled, he often finds himself scanning for the nearest door or trying to quiet his breathing before anyone notices. He dislikes being touched unexpectedly, especially from behind. Even now, he can react with a jolt that feels out of proportion to the moment, and then feel embarrassed by how long it takes his body to settle.

He also notices how often he tries to keep distress out of sight. In meetings, he is composed and efficient, but if a conversation becomes tense, he can feel himself shutting down internally. At work, when a system fails unexpectedly, colleagues may see him as focused and methodical, but inside he may be pulled back into the old helplessness of childhood—an old fear that something is going wrong and he will be blamed before he is helped. He double-checks his work, rechecks locks, and prefers routine because routine feels safer than improvisation. He sleeps lightly. Some nights he wakes with a sense of dread that takes several minutes to place in the present. He does not often describe nightmares in dramatic terms; instead, he says he wakes “already braced,” as if his body has been on watch all night.

He and his wife have built a good life, and he is aware of how much he cares for her. Even so, intimacy can be complicated by the old lesson that closeness can become unsafe quickly. He can be affectionate and thoughtful, but he sometimes goes quiet after conflict, needing distance before he can speak. He dislikes feeling trapped in emotional exchanges and may withdraw rather than risk saying the wrong thing. When he does talk about his childhood, it comes in fragments, with pauses that suggest he is checking whether the room is still safe enough to continue.

What stands out most is the way his history has shaped his present posture toward the world: alert, restrained, and always preparing for the possibility of pain. He has built a life of remarkable functioning around an inner expectation of threat, and even now, in a stable marriage and established career, the past remains close enough that ordinary moments can still carry its shadow.
